Hatchlings of the Mountain firetail emerge with a very modest body mass; newly hatched chicks weigh approximately 1.2 grams [Ww0 = approximately 1.2 grams]. This initial wet weight, measured shortly after the chick breaks free from the calcareous egg, is among the lowest recorded for estrildid finches of comparable adult size. The altricial nestling begins its development in a state of near-complete dependence on parental provisioning. Based on the closely related zebra finch Taeniopygia guttata, the incubation period for this species is estimated to be about 15 days [ab = about 15 days] when eggs are maintained at a stable temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C]. During this embryonated egg phase, the fertilised ovum develops within a protective albumen-buffered environment. Upon hatching, the chick undergoes a critical trophic switch, moving from reliance on the internal yolk reserves to its first exogenous feeding, which is provided by both parents through beak gape feeding. The nestling period is characterized by rapid feather growth and substantial mass gain.

As the nestling matures, it transitions into a pin-feathered chick before eventually achieving its first flight. The time since birth at fledging for the Mountain firetail is calculated to be 17.5 days after hatching [tx = 17.5 days after hatching], a value also derived from comparative data on Taeniopygia guttata when rearing conditions are held at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This developmental milestone marks the end of the nest-dependent chick stage and the beginning of the post-fledging dispersal phase. At fledging, the young bird is still reliant on its parents for food but gains nutritional independence over the subsequent days. The growth trajectory during the nestling phase is steep, reflecting the high metabolic demands of developing flight feathers and a functional endothermic physiology. Once the fledgling achieves parental independence, it enters a juvenile stage as an immature bird, typically forming small flocks with other first-year birds. This pre-reproductive juvenile period is critical for learning foraging skills and establishing a territory in the highland forests of New Guinea that the species inhabits.

Reproductive maturity in the Mountain firetail is attained after a specific period of somatic growth and gonadal development. Puberty, characterized by the onset of gametogenesis and a surge in reproductive hormones, occurs at 52.5 days after hatching [tp = 52.5 days after hatching] when the birds are maintained at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This value represents the time since birth at which the developing juvenile becomes a reproductively viable organism. Following the attainment of sexual maturation, individuals do not typically begin breeding immediately. The time since birth at first brood, or the age at first successful reproduction, is approximately 365 days since birth [tR = approximately 365 days since birth] under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay of nearly a year between puberty and first breeding is likely an adaptive strategy, allowing young birds to accumulate sufficient body condition and secure a high-quality nesting territory in the competitive montane environment. Birds that attempt to breed earlier may face reduced success due to inexperience or poorer physical condition.

Female Mountain firetails ultimately reach an adult body mass of approximately 18.45 grams [Wwi = approximately 18.45 grams], which represents the ultimate wet weight for females in this species. This asymptotic mass is substantially greater than the hatchling weight, reflecting the considerable biomass accumulated during the growth and maturation phases. The reproductive output of a breeding adult female is constrained by both clutch size and the frequency of nesting events. Females typically lay between 2 and 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 2 and 5 eggs per clutch], with a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch produced each year]. This annual reproductive rate is modest compared to some lowland passerines, a pattern consistent with the slower life-history pace often observed in high-altitude specialists. The energy required to produce a clutch of eggs represents a significant physiological investment for a bird of this body size, and the 1.2 gram initial mass of the hatchling reflects the limited egg volume available for yolk and albumen storage.

A comprehensive physiological profile of the Mountain firetail reveals a resting metabolic rate that is typical for a passerine of its size. Measurements of basal oxygen consumption indicate a maximum BMR of 29.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 29.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when assessed at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This metabolic rate supports the high energetic costs of thermoregulation in its cool montane habitat. In terms of overall longevity, the maximum lifespan recorded for this species under field conditions is estimated at approximately 8.6 years [am = approximately 8.6 years] when the birds live at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This lifespan is relatively long for a small granivorous finch and likely reflects the low extrinsic mortality rates associated with a stable, predator-limited highland environment. The combination of a modest reproductive rate, a long lifespan, and a delayed age at first reproduction positions the Mountain firetail as a slow-recovering species, sensitive to habitat disturbance.
